articles.title: In 2010, a British anthropologist launched a small Copenhagen beekeeping project to help people facing exclusion from work; today it spans 80 to 100 urban colonies producing up to six tonnes of honey a year
articles.summary: What started in 2010 as a small social project on a Copenhagen rooftop has grown into a successful urban business.
articles.body: What started in 2010 as a small social project on a Copenhagen rooftop has grown into a successful urban business. Today, it manages between 80 and 100 bee colonies across the Danish capital and produces up to six tonnes of honey each year. The project, called ByBi (CityBee), was started by British anthropologist Oliver Maxwell. His aim was to build a social enterprise that helps people who face social and economic barriers. It does this by training people who have been unemployed for a long time, asylum seekers, and people recovering from addiction in beekeeping. According to a report by The Guardian, the project offers an alternative to traditional business models. It uses work with nature to help people from disadvantaged backgrounds rebuild their confidence and develop new skills.Combining environmental care and social inclusionByBi places beehives in different parts of Copenhagen, including on the rooftops of company headquarters, in public parks, on housing estates, and at cultural institutions. The project works with local businesses, city authorities, and community groups. Companies can sponsor beehives on their premises, while ByBi takes care of the bees, collects the honey, and processes it. In an interview with The Guardian, Maxwell explained that the project was created to question common ideas about productivity and the value of people's work. “We created ByBi to explore how a business can create value for people, nature, and the city simultaneously,” Maxwell told The Guardian. “The bees are a great metaphor, but they are also very real worker partners. They show how small, daily contributions can build something massive and beneficial for the whole community.” People who join the programme receive practical training in caring for beehives, collecting honey, packaging products, and selling them. By offering flexible work in a less stressful setting, the organisation helps people who have spent years outside the regular job market take steps towards employment.Scaling up urban productionOver the past 15 years, ByBi has greatly expanded its work across Copenhagen. It now manages a network of beehives that produces between four and six tonnes of honey each year. The amount depends on seasonal weather and when flowers bloom. The honey varies by neighbourhood because each area has different plants and flowers. These include coastal parks and botanical gardens. ByBi packages and sells the locally produced honey through markets, shops, and corporate partners. The organisation also makes beeswax candles, honey-based sweets, and cosmetics. These products create more jobs in processing and packaging for programme participants during the winter months, when the bees are less active and the hives are dormant. Data from ByBi cited by The Guardian shows that hundreds of people who faced barriers to finding work have taken part in the programme since 2010. Many have gone on to find permanent jobs or enter formal education.Rethinking economic value through natureThe project is built around what Maxwell calls a "relational economy". This approach puts the health of the environment and people's well-being ahead of making the highest possible profit. Maxwell explained that traditional economic measures often treat social care and environmental protection as expenses rather than valuable investments. “The modern economic system often treats people and nature as resources to be extracted,” Maxwell said in statements reported by The Guardian. “What we are demonstrating is that when you structure an enterprise around care, inclusion, and biodiversity, the commercial outcomes follow naturally.” The project's success has attracted international interest from city planners, social activists, and environmental groups. They are exploring ways to use a similar model in other European cities. By placing beehives in different urban areas, ByBi also supports local wildlife and pollination. Its work helps maintain green spaces across Copenhagen while creating lasting routes into employment for people who face social and economic challenges.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: A 9-year-old Florida girl worried her wheelchair would get in the way of her Halloween dream; 25 eighth-grade STEM students turned it into an angel throne with wings, lights and her favourite colours
articles.summary: For nine-year-old Kaelyn Goodman, choosing a Halloween costume was not simply about finding the right dress or accessories.
articles.body: For nine-year-old Kaelyn Goodman, choosing a Halloween costume was not simply about finding the right dress or accessories. The Florida schoolgirl wanted to become a “princess angel”, but she was worried about how her wheelchair would fit into the costume. A group of 25 eighth-grade students at her school came up with a solution that allowed her to take part in the celebrations exactly as she had imagined.According to People Magazine, Kaelyn, who studies in fourth grade at Babcock Neighborhood School in Florida's Charlotte County, has congenital myasthenic syndrome (CMS). According to the Mayo Clinic, it is a rare genetic condition affecting the nerves and muscles. Kaelyn uses a wheelchair when her muscles become tired, and her parents say it helps her remain independent.Instead of treating the wheelchair as something that needed to be hidden, the older students made it the centre of her Halloween costume. They designed an angel throne around it, complete with wings, while allowing Kaelyn to choose how she wanted it to look. Their work was completed in time for the school's annual Trunk-or-Treat event on October 10.The result delighted Kaelyn, who told People that she particularly loved the wings and seeing her own suggestions included in the design. “They made my wheelchair into a beautiful angel throne, and I got to be a princess angel just like I wanted,” she said.How 25 students brought Kaelyn's Halloween idea to lifeThe costume was developed through Babcock Neighborhood School's Project-Based Learning initiative, which encourages students to apply classroom lessons to practical situations.The 25 eighth graders were studying science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM). Their assignment involved more than designing an attractive costume. They had to work out how to turn Kaelyn's idea into something she could actually use.The students, who later began calling themselves “Kaelyn's Angels”, also had an important participant in their discussions: Kaelyn herself.Lori McLain, the school's STEM director and teacher, told People that Kaelyn regularly spent time with the older children while they worked on the design. She was so interested in the project that she sometimes gave up her recess to join them.McLain said the students had to make adjustments when certain ideas did not work. They also learnt new skills, including sewing, during the process.Kaelyn's parents appreciated studentsKaelyn's parents, Jabori and Kathryn Goodman, said what mattered most was the way the students involved their daughter in the project.The couple, who are both retired service members, told People that ensuring Kaelyn can participate in everyday childhood experiences is something they think about regularly.They explained that the students did not assume they knew what Kaelyn would enjoy. Instead, they asked about her favourite colours, discussed her ideas and listened to her preferences before completing the costume, which was great as , according to Kaelyn's parents, she has strong opinions about what she wants.They also described their daughter as funny, affectionate, outgoing and imaginative. She enjoys being around people, making friends and participating in activities. Although her medical condition makes certain things more difficult, they said she remains determined to enjoy the same experiences as other children.Kaelyn wears her dream costumeOn October 10, Kaelyn attended the school's Trunk-or-Treat celebration dressed as the princess angel she had wanted to be. Her wheelchair had been transformed into a throne, with the design reflecting the ideas she had shared during the project.Kaelyn told People that she enjoyed dressing up, meeting people, and showing off the costume. She was especially pleased that others could see what the eighth-grade students had created for her.Babcock Schools Executive Director Shannon Treece said the experience reflected the importance of connecting education with situations in which students can make a difference to others.For Kaelyn's parents, the project showed that the students had looked beyond their daughter's medical condition and taken the time to understand what she wanted. According to them, eighth graders could have treated the costume as another school assignment, but instead made the experience personal by involving Kaelyn throughout the process.Meanwhile, Kaelyn herself said, “Sometimes people need help doing things, and it’s nice when someone cares enough to help. The eighth graders made me really happy.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Man held after three Jewish women report assaults in Hackney
articles.summary: Three women, one pushing a baby in a pram, reported being assaulted in Clapton Common, Hackney.
articles.body:
A man has been arrested after three Jewish women, one of whom was pushing a baby in a pram, reported being assaulted in north-east London.

Police were called to the Clapton Common area of Hackney at about 13:40 BST on Monday after a man had been detained by members of Shomrim, a Jewish neighbourhood watch group.

Officers arrested a 33-year-old man on suspicion of racially aggravated common assault. The women are believed to have suffered minor injuries.

The Metropolitan Police said it was treating the incident as a suspected antisemitic hate crime and had increased patrols in the area.

The man has since been further arrested on suspicion of grievous bodily harm in connection with a separate incident in Islington on Friday, the force said. He remains in custody.

Ch Insp Erica Crawshaw said it had been "an alarming and distressing incident" and thanked Shomrim volunteers for detaining a suspect before officers arrived.

"We recognise the concern that this incident will have caused the Jewish community here in Hackney," she said.

"We have increased patrols in the area and we are speaking to community leaders to provide further reassurance."

The Met has appealed for anyone with information, or anyone else who believes they may have been assaulted, to come forward.

articles.title: First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth promises to look at Welsh council powers
articles.summary: Plaid Cymru's leader makes pledge ahead of talks with Andy Burnham, who wants more devolution to councils.
articles.body:
The Welsh government is to examine the powers councils have and how authorities work together regionally, the first minister has announced.

At a speech at Cardiff University, Rhun ap Iorwerth announced that this could lead to new legislation after the next election in 2030.

He is due to meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who says ministers in Cardiff should hand more powers to local authorities, later this month.

Ap Iorwerth denied offering a quid pro quo to the prime minister, who the Plaid Cymru leader is hoping will give the Cardiff government more powers and funding.

In the same speech, he also called on the UK government to stop duplicating the Welsh government's economic development work.

"Where power can sit as closely to the people it affects, it should," the first minister said at the event at Cardiff University's Glamorgan building.

"Whilst I am clear that we should never assume that what works for England will work for Wales, and vice versa - and I hope the prime minister acknowledges this – I know that our current arrangements aren't perfect either.

"I am convinced that, over time, Wales should move towards a more coherent and more streamlined system of local and regional governance.

Ap Iorwerth promised a green paper by the end of the term, followed by the "option" of new legislation from the next Welsh government.

He said he wanted to be in a "good position to reflect on what is working and where change is needed" by the end of the term, but said the "conversation" had to start before then.

The first minister said it would be a "detailed, meaningful exercise reflecting on where powers and specific competences should lie, how regional working works best and what effective cooperation looks like".

Rhun ap Iorwerth has previously written to the prime minister calling for Wales to have the same powers as Scotland - including on railways, policing and justice.

Asked by BBC Wales if he was trying to offer the prime minister a "quid pro quo", ap Iorwerth said: "I don't quite see it in that way.

"As somebody who wants power close to the people in Wales, I like the fact that the UK's new prime minister is talking that kind of language, but it means different things in Wales and England.

"The devolution programme that we're hearing from Andy Burnham is largely an England programme. What I want to do is find common ground with him."

The first minister questioned whether Downing Street's "devolution agenda" was "really an England-only agenda", and whether it came to a "shuddering halt at Offa's Dyke".

Economic development in Wales is devolved to the Welsh government.

But ap Iorwerth said Wales was living with a "confused" and "increasingly fragmented system".

"A succession of UK government programmes has been layered on top of devolved responsibilities and in some cases undermining them," he said.

"Some have funded worthwhile projects. Some have brought genuine benefits. But, taken together, they have made the landscape more complicated, more fragmented and more difficult to navigate."

He listed city and growth deals, and the former Conservative UK government's levelling up and shared prosperity fund projects, as examples.

"If powers have been devolved, central government should not continue to duplicate them," he said.

He called for a "practical agreement about how our two governments work together to unlock Wales' economic potential".

Asked later to clarify, he said he was not saying he wanted to get rid of city and growth deals - agreements between the UK government, Welsh government and local councils to help fund local projects - of which there are four in Wales.

"Whatever we have, lets look at what works well and how we can improve it," the first minister said.

articles.title: Yankees all-star CC Sabathia helps fund $11 million ‘Harlem Field of Dreams’; renovated Brigadier General Charles Young Playground field now serves five sports
articles.summary: CC Sabathia, the former New York Yankees pitcher, has helped transform a dilapidated dirt field in Harlem into a place where children can play.
articles.body: CC Sabathia, the former New York Yankees pitcher, has helped transform a dilapidated dirt field in Harlem into a place where children can play. Through his PitCCh In Foundation, Sabathia joined public agencies and sports organisations to fund the $11 million Harlem Field of Dreams at Brigadier General Charles Young Playground. The renovated field now accommodates five sports, offers free youth programming, and honours a remarkable figure in American military history. Here is how the project was paid for, what the new field offers local families, and why the history of the playground and its surroundings matters to the neighbourhood.How the $11 million Harlem Field of Dreams was funded, asset forfeiture money and foundation donationsAccording to a 2025 press release from the Office of the Mayor of New York City, the $11 million project drew on several funding sources. Roughly $7.5 million came from law enforcement asset forfeiture funds from the New York and New Jersey High Intensity Drug Trafficking Area program, in partnership with the New York City Police Department and the New York City Police Foundation. Additional contributions came from Sabathia's PitCCh In Foundation, Major League Baseball, the Major League Baseball Players Association Youth Development Fund, the National Football League Foundation Grassroots Program, the Cal Ripken Senior Foundation, the Manhattan Borough President's Office, and the New York City Council. The release does not say how much each partner gave, so Sabathia's exact share is not specified.Five sports, more than 800 young players, and new amenities on the renovated Harlem athletic fieldThe project turned a dilapidated dirt field into a 150,000 square foot synthetic turf field built for multiple sports. Eric Adams, then mayor of New York City, told the public in the release that more than 800 young people can now play baseball, football, soccer, and lacrosse there. The city says the field accommodates five sports in total, with softball completing the list. Upgrades include improved drainage and water detention, drinking fountains, fencing, backstops, benches, dugouts, and a sports mister. The release describes a $9 million transformation, while the mayor's remarks and later sections cite $11 million for the full project. Sabathia told the public that giving back has always been at the heart of everything he does, and that New York has become his second home.Free Saturday Night Lights programming and a public safety approach that keeps young people engagedThe city plans to offer free youth sports on the new field through the New York City Department of Youth and Community Development's Saturday Night Lights program, which the release describes as a way to give young people safe places to play while building trust between law enforcement and communities. The field is part of an upstream approach to public safety that invests in free programming to keep young people engaged when they are not in school. Earlier improvements in 2023 included new asphalt and fencing for the main basketball court, repairs to three basketball courts, and the conversion of one court into a soccer pitch. The field house bathrooms are also set for upgrades with $2.5 million in public funding.Brigadier General Charles Young, the history behind the Harlem playground and the Hellfighters armouryThe playground is named for Brigadier General Charles Young, who was born into slavery in Kentucky in 1864 and became the third Black graduate of the United States Military Academy at West Point. According to the release, he served more than 30 years in the United States Army and became the first African American colonel before being forced into medical retirement in 1917. To prove his fitness, he rode 497 miles on horseback to Washington, though his appeal failed, and he was posthumously promoted in 2022. The playground sits just north of the 369th Regiment Armoury, home to the Harlem Hellfighters, a regiment that saw more combat than any other unit during World War One. Cal Ripken Junior told the public that the field is the 125th Youth Development Park, opened by the Cal Ripken Senior Foundation.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Former Biden aide predicts socialists will be sidelined in 2028, 'Baby gets put in a corner'
articles.summary: Third Way senior fellow Yemisi Egbewole predicts the Democratic Socialists of America will be sidelined ahead of 2028 despite recent primary wins.
articles.body: Former Biden White House aide and Democratic strategist Yemisi Egbewole predicted that the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) would be sidelined ahead of the 2028 presidential election during a Wednesday episode of "The Fifth Column" podcast, hosted by Kmele Foster and Michael Moynihan, despite the socialist movement's recent primary victories. When asked by Foster whether the Democratic Party was moving toward the DSA's ideology, Egbewole, a senior fellow at the centrist Democratic think tank Third Way, predicted the movement would struggle to translate its recent successes into national influence. "Going into 2028, the DSA... Baby gets put in a corner," Egbewole said. CARVILLE WARNS DEMOCRATS MAY NEED TO BLOCK FAR-LEFT CANDIDATES FROM JOINING CAUCUS, MODERATE GROUP DISAGREES Egbewole acknowledged that socialist-backed candidates had performed well in recent Democratic primaries but questioned whether those victories reflected broader support for the movement among voters nationwide. "Anybody running to represent America is not going to seek anybody who's a part of the DSA," Egbewole added. Republicans rejected the suggestion that Democrats could distance themselves from socialism ahead of the next presidential election. RNC national press secretary Natalie Baldassarre criticized the party's ideological direction in a statement to Fox News Digital. "It's too late for Democrats to rewrite their socialist brand," she said. "They've embraced socialism with open arms, and every 2028 Democrat contender is a tax-hiking, open border radical who will eagerly bend over for the far-left base." RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA Curtis Houck, managing editor of media watchdog NewsBusters, was also skeptical of Egbewole's claim. "The train seems to have left the station," he told Fox News Digital. "The liberal, elitist media are deathly terrified of their base voters. The red-green alliance is a tidal wave the press sure don't seem interested in litigating. They will either downplay the aims of DSA, or ignore them. Neither seems to be a winning strategy." Egbewole's comments followed a series of primary victories by candidates aligned with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. In June, three Mamdani-backed candidates swept Democratic congressional primaries in New York, with Brad Lander and Darializa Avila Chevalier unseating Reps. Dan Goldman and Adriano Espaillat, respectively, and Claire Valdez winning an open-seat contest. During the podcast appearance, Egbewole downplayed the ideological significance of those victories, arguing that defeating established Democrats did not necessarily amount to defeating moderates. RAHM EMANUEL CHALLENGES DSA’S INFLUENCE ON DEMOCRATS, WARNS GOP ‘WING’ IS DISAPPEARING "I'm okay with admitting they did well," she said. "They won their races. They didn't really defeat moderates . . . Dan Goldman wasn't a moderate." Egbewole's own organization, Third Way, works to limit socialist influence within the Democratic Party. The centrist organization had launched a $15 million campaign targeting the DSA through 2028, including opposition research, polling and outreach to Democratic leaders. Third Way co-founder Matt Bennett previously explained why the organization considered the socialist movement a threat to the party's electoral prospects. "We believe the DSA poses a serious threat to Democrats," Third Way co-founder Matt Bennett said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "Their ideas are dangerous, and their politics are toxic. If we are to beat MAGA Republicans, we cannot allow our party to be defined by radicals." The ideological battle also extended into Michigan, where progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated moderate Rep. Haley Stevens in August's Democratic primary. Egbewole suggested that even a victory by a DSA-adjacent candidate would not necessarily establish the movement's broader electoral strength. "I say if it's anything less than like five points, then it doesn't count," Egbewole said. The divide has also reached prominent Democrats considering their political futures. California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a potential 2028 presidential contender, said in September that Democrats were "pretty aligned" with the DSA on several policy priorities, including universal healthcare and climate change. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Meanwhile, Mamdani faced pressure from socialist allies over his governing decisions. The mayor said Thursday he had no plans to fire NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch despite calls from the Democratic Socialists of America's New York City chapter for her removal following an ICE-involved shooting in the Bronx. The DSA previously defended its growing political influence after Third Way announced its campaign against the organization. DSA co-chair Megan Romer said in an August statement to Fox News Digital that the group intended to continue organizing despite the opposition. articles.title: In 2016, Jennifer Lawrence donated $2 million to a children's hospital in her Kentucky hometown; four years later, a 17-room cardiac intensive care unit opened after the campaign raised more than $4 million
articles.summary: In 2016, Academy Award-winning actor Jennifer Lawrence donated $2 million to Norton Children's Hospital in Louisville, Kentucky, to help establish a
articles.body: In 2016, Academy Award-winning actor Jennifer Lawrence donated $2 million to Norton Children's Hospital in Louisville, Kentucky, to help establish a specialised cardiac intensive care unit for children. The gift also came with a challenge to the community to contribute towards the project, helping the fundraising campaign raise more than $4 million. According to official updates published by Norton Children's Hospital, the Jennifer Lawrence Cardiac Intensive Care Unit was dedicated in December 2019, and its first patients moved in early 2020. The 17-room facility was designed to provide specialised treatment for children with serious heart conditions.A donation inspired by her hometownLawrence, best known for films including The Hunger Games and Silver Linings Playbook, grew up in Louisville, Kentucky. Her connection to the city remained important as her acting career developed, and she chose to support institutions serving children and families in her hometown. According to Norton Healthcare's September 2016 announcement, the Jennifer Lawrence Foundation made a $2 million gift in February that year to establish the cardiac intensive care unit. The donation was intended to strengthen specialised heart care at Norton Children's Hospital, where young patients undergo complex procedures and require intensive monitoring.Lawrence also challenged other donors to contribute an additional $2 million. The appeal encouraged members of the community to participate in the project rather than relying on one contribution alone. The campaign ultimately raised more than $4 million through the Children's Hospital Foundation, providing support for the new unit. The initiative demonstrated how a major individual donation, combined with community fundraising, could help a hospital expand its specialised facilities.Why the hospital needed a dedicated cardiac unitChildren with congenital heart defects and acquired heart conditions may require surgery, intensive monitoring and extended hospital stays. Some undergo open-heart surgery or heart transplants, while others need treatment for heart failure and related complications. articles.title: Danielle Bernstein sold part of WeWoreWhat for eight figures before turning 30; years later, she has bought back a stake as the brand relaunches
articles.summary: Danielle Bernstein, the founder of fashion brand WeWoreWhat, sold a stake in her company for eight figures before turning 30.
articles.body: Danielle Bernstein, the founder of fashion brand WeWoreWhat, sold a stake in her company for eight figures before turning 30. Now, 15 years after starting the platform, she has bought back a stake in the business as she prepares to reposition the brand. Bernstein discussed the decision on the October 14, 2026, episode of the Hot Smart Rich podcast and in a paid Substack essay published the following day. The buyback coincides with a wider relaunch that gives WeWoreWhat a separate social media identity and introduces a more clearly defined premium offering. Although the exact financial terms of the original sale and subsequent buyback remain private, her account offers a look at how an influencer-built business is evolving into a more independent fashion company.Danielle Bernstein’s eight-figure WeWoreWhat stake sale and buybackBernstein founded WeWoreWhat in 2011, initially using the platform to share personal style and street-style content. What began as a blog developed into a fashion business selling clothing and accessories. Before turning 30, Bernstein sold a portion of the company to her production partner, who became a co-owner. On Hot Smart Rich, Bernstein discussed the financial benefits of selling part of the company early in her career and reflected on why she considered the decision worthwhile.Importantly, Bernstein said she retained creative control after selling the stake. Podcast host Maggie Sellers Reum also explained that Bernstein had maintained majority control of the company. The subsequent buyback gave Bernstein a way to consolidate her ownership as she reconsidered the company’s future. However, the publicly available reporting does not specify the ownership percentage she held before the buyback or how much her stake increased. In her October 15 Substack essay, titled I sold part of my company before 30. Then I bought it back, Bernstein discussed her decision to repurchase equity in WeWoreWhat. The essay’s public summary says she discusses why she originally sold part of the business, what she did with the proceeds and why she decided to invest in the company again. The full essay is available to paid subscribers. Neither the price paid to repurchase the stake nor the complete terms of the transaction have been publicly disclosed. The Glam Letter reported that Bernstein bought back the stake late the previous year, but it did not provide the financial terms of the deal.WeWoreWhat relaunch introduces premium materials and a separate brand identityThe ownership change coincides with a broader relaunch. According to FashionUnited, the rebrand introduces a new creative identity, more elevated materials and a clearer distinction between WeWoreWhat and Bernstein’s personal profile. The company’s social media account is moving from @shopweworewhat to @weworewhat, while Bernstein’s personal account is becoming @daniellebernstein. The separation is intended to help the brand establish its own identity rather than depending primarily on its founder’s following. The relaunch also expands WeWoreWhat Premium. FashionUnited reported that the autumn 2026 collection would grow from an initial two-style test to 11 pieces using materials including genuine suede, leather and pony hair, with prices below $800. The broader business continues to span ready-to-wear, denim, swimwear, outerwear and accessories.In the relaunch announcement, Bernstein said buying WeWoreWhat back gave her the opportunity to apply what she had learned and think bigger about the brand’s future. The repositioning also comes after years of criticism over allegations that some WeWoreWhat designs closely resembled work by other designers. Bernstein had previously denied accusations of copying. In the relaunch announcement, however, she acknowledged that the brand had sometimes failed to draw a clear enough line between inspiration and getting too close to another designer’s work. She also said the business had strengthened its design-review process. The new identity and premium collection are part of the company’s response, although whether they will rebuild consumer and industry trust remains to be seen.What the buyback reveals about founders, equity and business growthBernstein’s experience highlights the distinction between selling a stake and giving up control of a business. A founder can bring in a partner, realise some of the company’s value and still retain significant decision-making authority. The precise arrangement depends on the terms of the deal, including voting rights, ownership percentages and creative or operational responsibilities. Her story also illustrates how a founder’s needs can change as a business grows. On Hot Smart Rich, Bernstein discussed the possibility of outgrowing a business partner and needing a different relationship to take the company to its next stage. She described the original sale as a positive decision while explaining why buying the stake back was another significant step.The brand’s relaunch points to a related challenge: turning a founder-led platform into a company that can succeed independently of its founder’s personal audience. In her free essay reflecting on 15 years online, Bernstein described her ambition for WeWoreWhat as “founder-led, not founder-dependent.” The distinction reflects her aim to build a brand whose appeal rests on its products and identity, rather than relying primarily on her personal following. That ambition is particularly relevant to creator-founded businesses, where personal visibility can drive early growth but may also make it difficult to separate the company from its founder. A distinct brand identity, stronger product development and clearer design processes could help WeWoreWhat build a more durable business, though the results will depend on how the changes are implemented. Bernstein’s buyback is not proof that selling equity early is always the right decision, or that founders can easily reverse such deals.It shows how ownership arrangements can change as a founder’s priorities and business strategy evolve. Bernstein’s next challenge is to demonstrate that the relaunch can give WeWoreWhat lasting appeal beyond her personal online presence.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
articles.summary: Penalties are seen as too harsh on motorists who are penalised for parking on private land.
articles.body:
Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.

The Prime Minister announced the changes after drivers repeatedly raised concerns penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly penalised.

In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped .

Private car parks already have an industry code of practice, but the RAC motoring group said the government's changes would protect drivers from the "poor practices of some private parking companies".

Burnham, the prime minister, said: "Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your numberplate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat.

"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them."

a guaranteed 5 minute period to decide whether to park

A 10 minute window to leave without facing a penalty

Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, like vehicle breakdowns in car parks

Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines

Maximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups like forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking

A freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice

Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it far more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.

Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets. RAC analysis of government data showed a record 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025/2026 - a 17% increase from a year earlier.

With each charge worth up to £100, the data, analysed by the Press Association and the RAC Foundation, suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.

The yellow and black envelope of a Penalty Charge Notice, or PCN, is a dreaded sight for motorists returning to their car.

The AA has warned some drivers pay up even if they have nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle. It said people felt they would not get a fair hearing if they appealed fines, with many saying they feared legal action.

The current private parking industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024.

But the culture of motorists feeling they have been harshly penalised has spurred the government to present a formalised code to Parliament.

The British Parking Association told the BBC it welcomed the changes, but said "many of the principles within the new framework are already reflected in the existing voluntary Code of Practice".

The new Code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales after motorists said they wanted independent oversight of the private parking industry.

Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said drivers "finally have something which could offer them better protections against the worst private parking operators". He said in the past they have "aggressively attacked drivers to the point where many simply pay up".

But the RAC's head of policy Simon Williams said it wasn't the leap his firm had been campaigning for. He called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of PCNs and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.

The government said it will be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendation from the Competition and Markets Authority.

articles.title: Hundreds of holiday lets operating without planning permission in Edinburgh
articles.summary: Hundreds of holiday-let properties are operating in Edinburgh despite being refused planning permission, new figures show.
articles.body:
Hundreds of holiday let properties are operating in Edinburgh despite being refused planning permission, new figures show.

Analysis from housing campaigners suggests that 800 of the 1,754 entire homes in the city which are licensed short-term lets (STLs) have had planning applications refused.

But because they have a licence they can continue advertising the properties through websites such as Airbnb.

Campaigners are calling for Edinburgh City Council to make more use of its enforcement powers, which include fining owners who do not have planning permission, while operators say STL laws introduced in 2023 are not working properly.

City of Edinburgh Council said its licensing policy was helping make sure holiday lets were safe and properly regulated.

The new laws were introduced to help tackle problems with housing demand and anti-social behaviour, especially in hot spots such as Edinburgh.

Anyone providing STL accommodation must have a licence or face a ban and fine of up to £2,500.

There are different licensing requirements depending on whether you are letting out a spare room or an entire property on a permanent basis.

Any STLs which started operating after the city introduced a control zone in September 2022 must also have planning permission if the owner does not live in the property on a regular basis.

The rules say that planning permission will also be needed for some residential properties which had already changed to a short-term let before that date.

Insiders from the industry claim the reality is that every full house is now expected to have planning consent - and that the majority of applications are rejected.

Living Rent and Leith Harbour & Newhaven Community Council carried out an analysis of the publicly available planning and licensing documentation.

This showed that on 6 September this year a total of 1,754 entire flats or houses had the relevant licenses.

The vast majority - 1,225 properties - did not have planning permission. This was either because they had not applied (in some cases it was not required) or it had been refused.

Of those properties with valid STL licences, 800 had been refused planning consent and not subsequently been granted it on appeal.

Despite this, these holiday lets can continue to operate until their licence is due for renewal, typically between one and three years after being issued.

Properties in residential tenements or located in areas of high concentration of short-term lets are among those being rejected for planning consent.

As with all breaches of planning laws, the council has the power to take action against STL owners operating without permission - but enforcement is not automatic and is carried out on a "reasonable and proportionate" discretionary basis.

Those applying for a licence in Edinburgh must either be in the process of applying for the correct planning permission or have it in place.

Campaigners claim some owners are "gaming the system" by submitting planning applications while applying for their licence but then withdrawing the planning application after the licence is secured.

Living Rent's analysis shows 465 of the licensed full property STLs have withdrawn a planning application once, with 110 having withdrawn more than one application.

Chas Booth is a Scottish Green Party councillor in Leith who sits on both the licensing and planning committees.

He said the council was not doing enough to enforce the planning and licensing system, and that the Scottish government's legislation was not fit for purpose.

"There is a massive loophole in the law, which hundreds of STL owners are exploiting, and which is causing misery for residents," he said.

"Scottish ministers need to wake up and smell the coffee. This legislation has a loophole as big as a barn door, and they need to take urgent action to close it."

Niall Robb, of campaign group Living Rent, said the council needed to step up its enforcement.

"For the majority of STLs to have insufficient planning permission demonstrates how landlords are taking advantage of weak legislation and a lack of enforcement to profit at the expense of tenants and neighbourhoods," he said.

"Increasingly, communities are being undermined at the hands of holiday-let landlords who only care about profit.

"As a result of their actions, residents who keep the city ticking over every day are being forced out by sky high rents and a lack of homes."

'Your stomach drops when you hear the suitcases'

Leith resident, Katie Beale, has had multiple incidents with guests staying in the STL in her stair.

"It's the constant noise, the constant turnovers, strangers in the hallway," she said.

"When you live here and you know your neighbours, you've all got your little routines and everyone's very considerate of each other.

"But your stomach just drops when you hear the wheelie suitcases coming up the street."

Beale said there had been instances of guests running up and down the hallways, pressing all the buzzers in the stair and throwing things out the window onto the street.

She added: "We have had to call the police with noise complaints. I suppose I'm quite resilient but it does wear you down because it's a constant turnover of new people. Who are you going to get is just a bit of pot luck."

"We definitely welcome visitors to Edinburgh," she added. "It's just they need to be in the right places."

Paul Phillips owns a holiday-let flat in Edinburgh city centre and is a non-executive director of trade body the Association of Scotland's Self-Caterers (ASSC).

His is one of the 800 properties which has a licence but was denied planning permission by the council.

"I'm now in a position where the property is licensed, it's running without causing any issues to my neighbours," he said.

"But my expectation is at some point it will shut down when I have to reapply for my licence because I don't have planning permission in place.

"This has already happened to many people within the city."

Philips estimated he had spent about £8,000 on trying to get all the relevant regulatory permissions for his business.

He said the current STL regulatory system was "very frustrating" for all interested parties.

He added: "It feels like an injustice to be honest.

"We have enough evidence now, both councils and operators, to understand what the problems are.

"I think it's sensible to take a step back, tweak the regulations, make sure that businesses that run without any issue that have been running for many years continue to run and those that are problematic or unsafe aren't allowed to run."

It is understood the City of Edinburgh Council currently has 329 active STL enforcement investigations.

Of these, 117 relate to licensed STLs and the remaining 212 are for unlicensed properties. Last year the first owner convicted of running an unlicensed STL in the city was fined £600.

A total of 32 cases - comprising 52 offences - related to STLs have been reported to Scotland's prosecution service.

City of Edinburgh Council leader Jane Meagher said: "Our STL licensing policy is helping to make sure holiday lets are safe and properly regulated.

"We're aware of the issue between licensing and planning, and our planning committee has agreed to write to the Scottish government to seek solutions.

"We've also taken on an additional six full-time members of staff to make sure operators have a licence in place."

Scotland's minister for public finance, Hannah Mary Goodlad, was last month asked in Holyrood if the legislation would be changed to ensure properties operating as short-term lets could not do so without planning permission.

She said: "Under existing licensing legislation, authorities may already refuse to consider a new licensing application if they believe that there has been a breach of planning control.

"Operating without planning permission, where required, is a breach of planning control. Planning authorities can already take enforcement action."

She added: "Scotland can already take pride in assuring guests that short-term let accommodation across the country meets consistent safety standards."

articles.body: A kitchen renovation has uncovered an unexpected piece of history in a historic house in Evanston, Illinois. Kate Pearce and her husband, Bill, were removing a built-in structure near a former butler’s pantry when they found a dusty, unopened envelope hidden inside the wall. The letter dated back to 1914, but its discovery raised an unexpected question about why it had remained concealed for more than a century.According to PEOPLE, the couple first learned the letter was written in Swedish after an Instagram follower identified the language and translated it. A day or two later, they noticed it was addressed to a neighbouring house rather than their own.Couple discovers an unopened letter hidden inside a wall during kitchen renovationKate Pearce and her husband bought their Queen Anne-style home in Evanston, Illinois, in January 2022. Built in 1899, the house attracted them with its original architectural details, including a turret, curved mouldings, and stained-glass windows. The couple began renovating the kitchen to make the historic property their own.As part of the work, they demolished the existing powder room and planned to move it into the former butler’s pantry. While removing a built-in structure to access the plumbing, they came across a dusty envelope inside the wall. Pearce described it as very dirty and dusty. Pearce said, “It was unopened and obviously very old”“It had four stamps on it that were obviously foreign. It felt almost criminal to open it, but we had to know what was inside!”A century-old Swedish letter reveals a mother’s letter to ElseThe couple initially had no idea what the envelope contained or which language the letter used. Pearce admitted that she had half hoped to find a wad of cash inside. Instead, the discovery turned out to be a letter dating back to 1914.She shared photographs of the find with her Instagram followers to see if anyone could identify the language. One person soon recognised the writing as Swedish and translated the letter.Pearce said, “The letter is quite long”“It was written to Else from her mother, and primarily discusses day-to-day life back in Sweden. She mentions that her father isn’t doing well and that his back has been acting up”.What did the address on the century-old envelope revealA day or two after finding the letter, Pearce and her husband noticed a crucial detail on the envelope. It was addressed to a neighbouring house rather than their own, offering a possible explanation for why it had remained unopened for so long. Pearce had initially assumed that the property’s original owners were Irish because of the Irish motifs throughout the house.She said, “Of course, the home could have sold between 1899 and 1914, but I think it’s more likely that this letter was never intended for our home at all.”Why Pearce decided to leave the historic letter in the housePearce regularly shares old-house renovations on social media as an interior designer and content creator. She posted about the letter and another unexpected discovery involving a pocket door. Both discoveries attracted widespread online attention. Despite the interest, Pearce wanted to keep the letter in the house where it had remained for more than a century.She said, “If it had been there for more than 100 years, I didn’t want to be the person to take it from that spot,”“Part of the social contract of living in a historic district is having a certain reverence for old homes, and respecting their history. I think framing the letter and placing it on the wall where it was found was a great way to honor the letter, and this home’s history.”You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: The singles choosing IRL dating events over apps
articles.summary: The BBC hears from people who think dating events are better value for money than dating apps.
articles.body:
Checking in at a dating event in a bar in Guildford, Olivia Miller-Davis is understandably apprehensive.

Even bringing a friend with her doesn't remove the awkwardness at the start of the night.

"It's always nerve-wracking when you're meeting new people," the 28-year-old admits before downloading an app that will match her to other daters based on their star signs.

This is speed dating 2026-style and Olivia, like many people we speak to, is here because she's fed up of "endlessly swiping" or as some describe it "app fatigue".

She says she hates judging people with "really limited information and just a couple of pictures" because she doesn't feel she can "really fully commit" with so little to go on.

According to a recent study from online regulator Ofcom 11% of adults use dating sites but it suggests the time we spend on them is dropping, from a peak of almost four hours a month in 2023, down to three hours last year.

Olivia's first match on the night is Edward and he agrees that recent dating trends leave him feeling cold.

"I mean, they're designed so that you don't find 'the one', because they want you to come back and use the app forever. They don't want you to get married from the app."

The event is organised by Love at First Sign, a dating company that uses an app to match people based on astrological connection, but most people are just using it as an icebreaker.

Director of events Lissy Cleminson says the way people date is changing and a big factor is more home working since Covid, which means people do not meet in offices or on the commute.

"The little meet-cutes don't happen so much when you're at home with your shirt up top and your pyjamas down bottom," she jokes.

As you may expect at a dating event many of the singles told us they were keen for that in-real-life or IRL experience.

There are a lot of #SingleTok and #Singlelife accounts on TikTok and Instagram reviewing dating events.

Candice Gallagher runs an account called @Candilicious and recently went to 10 different dating events in 10 weeks.

She describes herself as an entrepreneur and thinks in business terms dating events deliver "much greater return on investment".

The 40-year-old says all too often dating online can lead to "chat graveyards" with very limited conversation.

"At a dating event, everyone is single, everyone's ready to mingle, and your chances of having a good conversation are much greater."

Many people at the event in Guildford agreed dating events were better value for money because "you get to meet a range of people" in person for a similar cost to one date from an app.

These events typically cost around £15 to £30 and often include a drink and activity or icebreaking gimmick, in this case an app that is used throughout the night.

Olivia believes money plays a big factor in dating.

"I wasn't working for a bit because I changed careers and because of that I put dating on hold."

Olivia remembers thinking it "couldn't be a priority" and feeling she needed to wait until she was "earning enough" before dating again.

She is not alone in finding dating expensive.

More than a quarter of daters surveyed by Barclays suggested rising costs had changed how they date.

And a couple of recent studies suggest the monthly cost of dating - from apps to entertainment and clothes - can add up to around £130.

Those running apps are quick to point out online is still a big part in the way people meet.

New research from Match Group, which owns Tinder and Hinge, suggests that out of those who had ever had a romantic relationship, about 21% of baby boomers surveyed met their most recent partner at a pub, bar or club.

The survey of 3,007 single people also suggests that of those who had ever had a relationship, 20% met their most recent partner on a dating app and 20% met through friends.

Chine Mmegwa, head of strategy, corporate development and operations at Match Group, said Tinder has made tweaks to its service in the past year to win back younger daters.

As well as helping users find out more about each other in advance of dates, through interactive music and astrology features, it has introduced "double date mode" for friends who want to date together.

And she said Tinder is doing more to encourage people to connect IRL. "They want to be in person. You've seen us launch events across the US and now the UK. We are bringing IRL experiences into the app.

"What we're doing is putting IRL into our experience. And so we are bringing that gap to what they're looking for in person, using the apps."

In Guildford, Olivia says her night was a success because she met some men she might want to go on a first date with.

When pushed by the BBC on whether she thought she had met "the one", she laughs and becomes understandably guarded.

"No, I'm not going to name anyone specific. But you'll be invited to the wedding if there is one!"

articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Who really controls the Lawrence Bishnoi network while its notorious kingpin is confined to a high-security cell inside Gujarat's Sabarmati
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Who really controls the Lawrence Bishnoi network while its notorious kingpin is confined to a high-security cell inside Gujarat's Sabarmati jail? The answer, sources told TOI, is that the gang is being run by a 'shadow cabinet' of Lawrence's key lieutenants who orchestrate transnational operations from foreign safe havens. The core group comprises Tyson Bishnoi, Anil Pandit, Hari Boxer, Harman Sandhu and Himanshu Sonipat. They coordinate recruitment, tasking and logistics, and share screenshots. A parallel group comprising Aarzoo Bishnoi, Shubam Lonkar and Randeep Malik handles planning, financing and target selection. Gangster Goldi Dhillon was also part of it but went underground after FBI launched Operation Hardball.Operating from the US, Canada and parts of Europe, the command structure oversees digital intimidation and field executions, directing local recruits through Signal, Instagram and WhatsApp.Sources said seasoned kingpins Rohit Godara and Goldy Brar retain control and have falsely projected a split with Lawrence to mislead investigators. "Operating from deep within international safe havens, these higher-tier masterminds provide the strategic oversight, financial backing and cross-border protection that shield the network's mid-level lieutenants," an investigator said.Pandit, their main public mouthpiece, posts gang manifestos and extortion warnings on social media. A native of Panipat, he travelled to US via Canada a year after Sidhu Moose Wala was killed. Himanshu recently claimed responsibility for a drive-by shooting targeting Haryanvi singer Diler Kharkiya's Range Rover in Sonipat and rival gangster Vinod Kana's killing outside Hisar court complex on Aug 20.While Tyson issues online warnings to public figures, Hari drives ground-level extortion, and Harman coordinates overseas logistics through local executioners.This distributed chain of command explains why an intercontinental dragnet led by FBI and its global allies has failed to paralyse the syndicate. articles.title: Oil-rich Alberta votes on Canada separation: All you need to know
articles.summary: Oil-rich Alberta is voitng on whether to begin a process that could eventually lead to its separation from Canada, putting the country's national unity to
articles.body: Oil-rich Alberta is voitng on whether to begin a process that could eventually lead to its separation from Canada, putting the country's national unity to the test.The non-binding referendum does not ask Albertans to vote directly on independence. Instead, the province's residents are deciding whether to remain part of Canada or initiate the legal process for a future binding referendum on separation. The vote is part of a wider ballot exercise covering 10 questions on immigration and constitutional issues.Although polls suggest most Albertans oppose independence, the referendum has brought a long-running separatist movement into the mainstream of provincial politics. Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has campaigned for national unity, while Premier Danielle Smith called the vote after mounting pressure from separatist supporters within her governing United Conservative Party, despite opposing separation herself.Why is Alberta considering separation?Alberta, home to about five million people, is Canada's energy heartland and holds a substantial share of the country's oil reserves. Its economy is closely tied to the oil and gas industry, making federal environmental and energy policies a longstanding source of friction with Ottawa.Separatists argue that successive federal governments have constrained Alberta's energy sector through regulations and that the province contributes more to the national economy than it receives in return. They also contend that Canada's political system favours Ontario and Quebec, where much of the country's population is concentrated, leaving Alberta with limited influence over federal decisions.What are Albertans voting on?The referendum consists of 10 separate questions, each printed on a numbered, colour-coded ballot and placed in a corresponding ballot box. The first nine require a yes-or-no answer, while the tenth asks voters to choose between remaining in Canada and beginning the legal process for a binding independence referendum.Five of the first nine questions concern immigration, including proposals to give Alberta greater authority to restrict immigration and limit access to certain social services. The remaining four concern constitutional issues, including proposed changes to voting requirements.More than 1.3 million Albertans had already voted through advance and special ballots before Monday's polling day, reflecting considerable interest in the outcome. However, voting was disrupted at more than 100 polling stations that failed to open on time. Some locations extended their hours to allow voters to cast their ballots, delaying the release of results until all polling stations had closed.Ballots are to be counted by hand, with officials given 48 hours to complete the process. The separation question will be counted first because of the intense interest in the result, with initial results expected in the early hours of Tuesday.What happens if Albertans vote for separation?A majority in favour of beginning the separation process would not make Alberta an independent country. Instead, it would put the province on the path towards a second, binding referendum, which Smith has said she would seek if the proposal receives majority support.Even then, independence would raise complex questions about the province's constitutional status, defence arrangements, currency, border controls and economic relationships with the rest of Canada. Separatist groups have published transition plans, but several practical and legal issues remain unresolved.An Angus Reid poll released ahead of Monday's vote found that 66% of Albertans intended to vote to remain in Canada. However, about three in five respondents believed the separatist movement would never disappear. Among those supporting a future binding referendum, many said their vote was intended to send a message to Ottawa rather than necessarily establish an independent country.Carney has urged Albertans to reject separation, arguing that national unity is particularly important as Canada faces US tariffs and Trump's repeated annexation rhetoric. His government has also sought to address some of Alberta's concerns by reversing certain environmental policies and supporting a proposed pipeline to expand oil exports to Asia.You use AI every day. articles.title: Fatima El Mansouri: What can Morocco's first female prime minister change for women?
articles.summary: Will Fatima El Mansouri advance women’s rights amid religious and political barriers?
articles.body:
The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.

Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.

He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.

Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.

El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.

El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.

The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.

Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.

One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."

Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.

Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.

A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.

However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.

While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.

Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.

Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances.

The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.

It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones.

In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.

Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.

But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.

These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody.

A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.

As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.

Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%.

"Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.

She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products.

"Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.

El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.

For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.

After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women.

"Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.

Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.

In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.

Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests.

"Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC.

"The latter cannot be understood without the former."

Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.

Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".

She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.

For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important.

"It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."

El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.

For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.

However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system.

The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.

When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.

While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts.

"I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.

"Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."

articles.title: Calgary Opera removes singer waving Palestinian flag during opening night curtain call
articles.summary: The Calgary Opera, a Canadian-based company, announced that it would be dropping Gabriel Sanchez-Ortega after he flew a Palestinian flag during his curtain call.
articles.body: The Calgary Opera removed a cast member from its remaining performances of "Tosca" after he displayed a Palestinian flag during the opera's opening-night curtain call Friday. Bass-baritone singer Gabriel Sanchez-Ortega pulled out the flag during the curtain call following the opening-night performance. The opera company later released a statement calling Sanchez-Ortega's actions "unexpected and unauthorized," confirming that he would be replaced for the remaining performances. "Individual political protest contravenes not only company policy, but also our responsibility to create a more connected, caring, and civil society through shared artistic experience," the statement read, according to OperaWire. "We recognize that this moment may have affected the audience — as well as cast members, crew, orchestral musicians, and Jubilee staff — in different ways, and we regret any discomfort and distress it caused." AUSTRALIAN POLICE INVESTIGATING PRO-PALESTINIAN RALLY IN SYDNEY WHERE PROTESTORS CHANTED ‘GAS THE JEWS’ "We have addressed this matter directly with the cast member and reinforced our expectations with the cast and production team," the statement continued. "Our commitment is to provide a welcoming and respectful environment for our artists, audiences, and community. The role of Angelotti will be performed by another artist for the remaining performances. We thank everyone who joined us for opening night and look forward to welcoming audiences to the remaining performances of ‘Tosca.'" Sanchez-Ortega, who posted a video of himself holding the flag on Instagram, released a statement saying he has "no regret" over his actions and claimed that Calgary Opera was faced with "financial threats" over the move. "I have been informed that I have been removed from further performances of ‘Tosca’ with the Calgary Opera following my display of the Palestinian flag during curtain call. I have no regret," he said. "This is the state of cultural institutions in Canada," Sanchez-Ortega wrote on social media. "I was informed that financial threats had been made against Calgary Opera. I hold no resentment. After the theatre, (political or otherwise) we all have to go home, and look at ourselves in the mirror. It was my honor to play the role of Angelotti, an escaped political prisoner." MACKLEMORE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER GETTING KICKED OFF ED SHEERAN TOUR AFTER PRO-PALESTINE STANCE In a statement to Fox News Digital, Calgary Opera declined to comment on "personnel matters" but added that all forms of personal protest, regardless of the political symbol, are prohibited on stage. "Calgary Opera prohibits personal protest on our stages and at our events," it said. "The display of any protest symbol or action would result in similar consequences. We have reiterated this prohibition to all artists and staff, and will continue to apply it universally in response to all cases of unauthorized protest, regardless of the symbol or action that protest takes." "With respect to the cast member in question, he did not appear in yesterday’s performance of Tosca, and will not appear in the October 24, 2026, closing performance," the statement added. "Beyond that, Calgary Opera does not comment on personnel matters." Working with Proyectos Retic, a group of python hunters in Puerto Rico who collect data and specimens about the reticulated python, Snakeaholic aka Kevin Pavlidis helped snag a reticulated python that measured 18' 4" long. This gigantic snake was held up by eight people standing shoulder-to-shoulder to show just how big of a snake they're dealing with. They tracked it down after it was "spotted strangling a pet cat behind a house."
